author: reek
body: At the back of a printed book there is a colophon: a short note saying who set the type, on what press, on what paper, in what month. It is the book describing its own making, and for five hundred years it has been the one page in the book that nobody could check. It says "Garamond" and you believe it, or you do not. It is a claim the artefact makes about itself, and the artefact is the only witness.

author: reek
body: A work stored in this repository is content-addressed, which is to say the work IS its hash. Change one byte of the text and it is a different work with a different name, and no amount of insisting otherwise will move it. So a colophon here can be checked: it states the hash of the work it belongs to, and anyone holding the work can recompute that hash and find out whether the colophon is lying.

author: reek
body: That is the whole of this chapter. It is a very old idea and a very short program.

author: reek
body: The hash is DERIVED here, never accepted. You cannot hand this function a hash to print, and that is deliberate: a colophon which repeats a hash it was given is precisely the unverifiable note we have had since Gutenberg. It takes the bytes and computes.

author: reek
body: The question a colophon has never been able to answer: is this note about THIS book? Hand it the work and the note, and it will tell you. It re-derives the hash from the bytes in front of it and looks for that hash in the note -- so a colophon copied from another edition, or edited after the fact, or simply optimistic, fails here.
